newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea union workers at Daewoo Motor plant strike.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea union workers at Daewoo Motor plant strike.

text.p: More than 10,000 unionised workers at a Daewoo Motors plant went on strike on Wednesday in South Korea's first major work stoppage since last winter's turmoil over controversial revisions to the country's labor laws.
The strike, which hit Daewoo's Bupyong plant west of Seoul, was called after negotiations broke down over wages and reinstatement of sacked employees.
"All assembly lines at the Bupyong plant stopped from 8:00 am (2300 GMT) and union members are holding rallies separately in several groups," said Daewoo spokesman Lee Chang-won.
Lee said the one-day strike would cost the company 1,600-1,700 vehicles in lost production.

Key South Korean industries were paralysed by strikes last January as workers protested a labour bill that would make layoffs, virtually unheard of in the country, easier. After weeks of militant strikes, the government watered down its legislation.
Analysts said the impact of the strike on Daewoo and other carmakers would be minimal unless it became protracted.

"In an early stage, the impact is quite limited because Daewoo Motors has enough inventory. But if the strike becomes prolonged, it will impact exports and the domestic side," said Kang Hoon-sok, motor analyst at ING-Barings.
Lee said the union would go back to work soon.
But the union, which has 10,171 members at Bupyong, plans to down tools for four hours for the next two days after a full one-day strike on Wednesday.
"We will suspend production lines from 10:00 am to 3:00 pm on Thursday and Friday," a union member said. The suspension includes workers' regular lunch hour.
The union has demanded a 9.7 percent rise in basic salary this year, while management has offered a 5.45 percent increase.

"We could not narrow our differences yesterday as management made no gestures to accommodate our demands and we walked out of a meeting. We don't have any plans to talk to management today," the union member said.
Daewoo's vehicle sales in the first half of this year totalled 461,977 units on the debut of new models including mid-sized sedan Leganza and smaller Lubira. It compared with 382,664 a year ago.
"The labour strife will affect potential buyers, who are trying to shy away from cars produced by striking companies on fears of possible defects," said Park Jae-suk, auto analyst at LG Securities.

The strike came at an especially bad time for Daewoo Motor, main automaking unit of Daewoo Group, which on Tuesday announced a recall of its Nubira sedans because of a potential electrical problem in the engine.
The company said 37 of 6,800 Nubiras sold in February were found to have a problem in the engine's electric control unit. Exports of the model began in March.
Analysts said Daewoo's labour problem, though small, could spread to other companies currently in wage negotiations.
"It's too early to say how the labour thing will turn out," Kang said. "But I'm worrying about the overall labour situation, as the Daewoo strike might affect other companies."
Labour uncertainty remained in Daewoo Heavy Industry, which makes mini-cars and ships and faces a possible strike next week if wage talks are not settled.

More worrisome is the situation at South Korea's largest carmaker Hyundai Motor, which is now in wage talks with its union. Hyundai workers have demanded a 9.87 percent wage increase, but management has made no counter offer yet.

"Next Tuesday is the deadline and we hope both the union and management can reach an agreement. But I cannot rule out the possibility that we will follow Daewoo's suit, if we fail," said a Hyundai Motor union member.
The union at Kia Motors Corp, hit by slumping sales, already agreed to let management to decide its pay rise.
